1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Recaptures with a developing move and takes over f3, keeping the queen at home. White is a pawn down but has the knight on its best square, a half-open f-file and a lead in development, and aims for a kingside attack.

Recaptures with the queen, which hits b7 and f6 at once, and offers the d4 pawn as a second sacrifice for development and attack. There is doubt that the compensation is enough for two pawns, and Black can also decline the offer.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Ryder Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..background: Most of the analysis in Diemer's late-1950s book Vom Ersten Zug An Auf Matt! is devoted to this double-pawn sacrifice.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Develops the c8-bishop outside the pawn chain before it can be shut in, and eyes c2. Black keeps the extra pawn and a sound structure, while White usually sets about harrying the bishop with the knight and kingside pawns.

A quiet, solid move that fixes a sturdy structure and prepares to develop the c8-bishop outside the pawn chain. Black keeps the extra pawn and aims to neutralise the initiative first; it is Black's most reliable set-up against the gambit.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Ziegler Defence
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..background: Diemer tended to name lines after opponents who first played them against him, and this one carries Ziegler's name; most of its theory was established by Gerhart Gunderam. Most modern authors recommend it as Black's antidote to the gambit.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop to add pressure on d4, especially once ...c5 follows. Black keeps the extra pawn in a compact set-up, and White has to prove the compensation with a precise kingside plan.

Aims for a solid pawn structure with an extra pawn, at the cost of shutting in the c8-bishop. White must prove its compensation, and a second pawn sacrifice has scored well in practice but probably does not give enough.

Pins the knight to the queen and prepares to trade it, which would remove a defender of d4 and weaken White's hold on the centre. White usually challenges the bishop at once, and the game can turn sharp.
Brings the queen out early to press on d4, but White gains time by attacking it with a minor piece. Black has the extra pawn, but the queen is more exposed than useful and the development lags.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Holwell Defence

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Strikes at d4 before developing. If White takes on c5, the d-file opens for a queen trade and Black has the pawn to win back, so the gambit's attack is blunted, but Black has spent time on a premature counterstrike.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Kaulich Defence

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Adds a second attacker on d4, but the knight can be pinned along the diagonal to the king, because d7 is empty. White gains time with the pin and the lead in development grows.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Pietrowsky Defence

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop on the long diagonal. A flexible but slow choice: it does not challenge d4 and lets White complete development with its initiative intact.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Ritter Defence

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..strategy: Develops the second knight and covers e5 and f6, but it blocks the c8-bishop and the d-file, so Black's pieces still have to untangle while White keeps developing with the initiative.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5..name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: Schlutter Defence
